author.name: Neil deGrasse Tyson
author.heading: About Neil deGrasse Tyson
author.bio: Neil deGrasse Tyson is an astrophysicist and public science communicator. His presentations have used anecdotes about science and public language, including a disputed recollection of a presidential reference to star names.

cite.sourceCitation: Tyson, Neil deGrasse. Recalled quotation in “I, Skeptic—Modern Skepticism in the Internet Age,”2008, transcribed by Wikiquote. Compare George W.Bush, “President Addresses Nation on Space Shuttle Columbia Tragedy,”February 1, 2003.

copyAttribution: — Words Tyson attributed to George W. Bush in a recollection; not verified Bush wording or Tyson’s own statement of belief.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The standalone attribution loses the speaker-within-a-speaker distinction. Tyson's reported context ↗ names Bush, while the actual Bush address ↗ has different language.

items.why: The standalone attribution loses the speaker-within-a-speaker distinction. Tyson's reported context ↗ names Bush, while the actual Bush address ↗ has different language.

misattribution.truthLine: Tyson quoted these words as something he remembered George W.Bush saying; they were not presented as Tyson's own creed. Bush's documented 2003 Columbia address uses different words about the Creator and the seven astronauts.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: A quotation can change meaning when the identity of the person supposedly being quoted disappears. Bush's actual Columbia address ↗ names the seven astronauts in a message of mourning, a different text and setting from the recollection embedded in Tyson's anecdote.

schema.webPageName: Who really said 'Our God is the God who named the stars'?
schema.claimReviewed: Neil deGrasse Tyson used these words as a recollection of a George W. Bush quotation, rather than his own statement of belief.
schema.verdictNote: Neil deGrasse Tyson is the documented reporting speaker of a recollection attributed to George W. Bush, not a confirmed originator or speaker of a personal creed. Bush’s actual Columbia address uses different wording; the exact original expression remains unconfirmed.
schema.faqAnswer: Tyson used these words while purporting to quote George W. Bush. They were not Tyson’s own declaration of belief, and they are not verified wording from Bush. The documented 2003 Columbia address uses different language.
